speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF DELEGATION FROM DAHOMEY
speechtext:
Order. Allow me to delay the routine proceedings of the house to point out to the hon. members the presence in the Speaker's gallery of a delegation from Dahomey.
That delegation, presided by His Excellency Dr. Emile Derlin Zinsou, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Dahomey, is composed of: His Excellency Mr. Louis Ignacio-Pinto, the permanent representative of Dahomey at the United Nations; His Excellency Dr. Nicolas Eouagnignon, the ambassador of Dahomey to Haiti; Mr. Frangois Covi, a member of the national assembly of Dahomey and chairman of the finance committee of that assembly; and Mr. Jules Laventure, secretary general of the ministry of foreign affairs.
These distinguished visitors will be in Canada for four days. They are visiting the capital today, and tomorrow they will go to Montreal and then to Quebec city.
I deeply regret that our Canadian capital is not in a position to welcome them better, on account of the weather, but since they have come to the snow country, we are able to give them ample evidence of what it is.
On behalf of the hon. members of the house I should like to welcome them and wish them a pleasant stay in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martineau (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF ASSISTANCE ON SHIPMENTS TO JAPAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to advise the house that during the 12 months commencing April 1, 1963, it is the government's intention to provide assistance on the movement to Japan of a limited tonnage of coal from western Canadian mines. This assistance will be at a maximum rate of $3.15 per ton, which is lower than the $3.50 maximum at present in effect. This provision is a continuation of the experimental investigation and development of this market undertaken some four years ago. The reports of the dominion coal board for 1957-58 and succeeding years outline this market development.
These show that starting with a trial delivery of some 48,000 tons in 1957-58, the quality of the coal was so acceptable that by
1959-60 some 263,000 tons were exported at a cost of $4.43 per ton in assistance. I should say here that an important part in this development was the dispatch to Japan of a technical mission composed of senior scientific officers of my department whose function it was to review, with the Japanese experts, the types and qualities of coal best adapted to their requirements. This was so successful that in 1960-61 some 677,000 tons were delivered and in 1961-62, 702,000 tons. These movements were assisted at a rate of $4.50 per ton. In the current year it is estimated that 700,000 tons will move at the reduced rate of assistance of $3.50 per ton, while next year the shipments will be in the order of
750,000	tons at $3.15 per ton.
The continued reduction in the rate of assistance from the earlier high of $4.50 per ton is evidence of the success of this experiment to date. The successive reductions have been due to the effective and continued efforts of the producers and the miners, supplemented by reduced handling rates by the railways

and the loading piers. Also, since the payment is made in U.S. funds the devaluation of the Canadian dollar has been a factor of considerable importance. If this trend continues it could be an element of some importance in any future consideration.

Is the incidence of tuberculosis, both by new active and reactivated cases, increasing in (a) Canada (b) each of the provinces (c) each of the territories; and, if so, by what degree in each case?

Tuberculosis incidence is measured through returns of provincial divisions of communicable disease control as part of the national notifiable disease reporting system. No distinction was maintained between active, inactive or reactivated cases in this notification system prior to 1961. However a rough estimate of the incidence of new active and reactivated cases based on analysis of the admission and discharge records of patients can be obtained from sanatorium statistics. The attached tables show the number and rates of active tuberculous first admissions and active tuberculous readmissions
Questions
in Canada, provinces and Northwest Territories for 1956 to 1960. Yukon statistics are not available for this period.
It will be seen that the total of active new cases and reactivated cases admitted to sanatoria in Canada has shown a steady decrease for each year since 1956.
Active tuberculous first admission rates show an increase for 1960 in four provinces, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Saskatchewan. However, the increases are very slight and are contrary to the general trend in these provinces. Similarly, the slight increases shown in the rates for 1961 in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Quebec and British Columbia may be ascribed to the inclusion in the notification system for the first time of cases not admitted to sanatoria but treated on a domiciliary basis.
Active tuberculous readmission rates show a decline in all provinces except New Brunswick which shows an insignificant increase in 1960. In 1961, dramatic declines appear to have taken place in the rates for reactivated tuberculosis. This is probably more apparent than real for in 1961, for the first time, the definition of a "reactivated case" was changed and to be included in this category required documentation of previous activity.

speechtext:
1 and 2. The figures on imports of automobile parts set forth in Hansard, page 519, were compiled from D.B.S. records according to the definition of "automobile parts" usually followed in preparing summaries of Canadian trade statistics. Within the limits of this definition (which was also included in Hansard), there is no discrepancy between the figures appearing in Hansard and those appearing in "Trade of Canada Imports" for December, 1961.
The value $29,374,410 appears to correspond to the total of five additional import statistical classes: 5242 "Engines, automobile and motor vehicle, and complete parts n.o.p., and stripped engines", 5245 "Engines, internal combustion, for motor trucks, motor buses, fire fighting vehicles, ambulances and hearses, and parts", 5682 "Bearings, ball and roller, and parts thereof, for automobiles", 7002 "Asbestos brake lining for road motor vehicles" and 7004 "Asbestos clutch facings for road motor vehicles". Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at ten o'clock last evening I was about to reiterate that in my humble opinion one of the most vital decisions facing this government is the extent of assistance the government is going to give to universities and industries for scientific research. The advent of science has brought about a new industrial revolution which is manifesting itself in the economic upsurge and the rising standard of living in western Europe. It has also brought to these countries mass production of automobiles, electrical appliances and other household commodities which are challenging our industries in markets both at home and abroad.
I respectfully submit, Mr. Chairman, that it is an elementary truth that if we are to remain competitive we must not only increase our output but we must increase it at a competitive price. I suggest that by the application of science to production we can lay the foundation to meet the challenge. I am not unmindful of the fact that an allowance of some $40,095,000 has been made available to the national research council. This, however, represents a cut-back of some $2,310,000 from the original estimates for the year ending March, 1963. In my humble submission, Mr. Chairman, this was a step in the wrong direction. Indeed, I believe that the original estimates were not large enough.
I am reinforced in that opinion by that respected authority, Dr. McGeer, of the University of British Columbia. I should like to read into the record a speech reported in the Vancouver Sun of Wednesday, October 3, 1962, in which Dr. McGeer stated:
-a string of research stations, patterned after the national research council, should be established across Canada.
He also said:
The establishment of research facilities would halt this flow of our brilliant and most educated people.
Indeed, if our facilities were of high quality- which they must be-then we might even be able to attract outstanding people from all over the world to come and contribute to the enrichment of Canada.
Then he said:
California estimates that for every dollar spent on research in its universities alone, it derives several dollars return as a result of improved earnings by industry from that research.
Our attention in recent months has been focused on power. Power is essential to development, but it can only be used if we develop the industrial genius to go with it.
It is small thinking to suppose that power alone is the key to our future.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, he said:
To keep pace with rival industrial countries, Canada must be prepared to undertake programs far bolder than anything previously conceived in the history of the nation.
The recent decision of the federal government to cut back on research expenditures was a blunder which will have further sorry consequences.

I concede that it would be distortion of fact to state that the federal government has not given valuable assistance to the provinces in establishing technical schools, but I suggest we should pay more attention to training on the job, with pay if necessary. It is not without significance that the Soviet union trains 130,000 skilled and semi-skilled

technicians each year. I believe that a true yardstick of our economy may be measured by the pool of skilled and semi-skilled help. In the last eight years more than 32,000 skilled and semi-skilled technicians have left this country for the United States.
I suggest, with respect, Mr. Chairman, that we might pick up the principle that we used during the war with the British commonwealth air training plan. It is within the memory of this house that thousands of raw, unskilled young men within two years were so ably trained that they were able to handle with great skill aircraft, radar equipment and other instruments requiring great technical knowledge. They not only were able to use it, but they were able to repair and maintain it with great efficiency. I realize that this system may pose great difficulties. However, I humbly suggest to the government for their consideration that we undertake a crash program to relieve the shortage of skilled and semi-skilled help. Here is one other aspect of the necessity of skilled help that is frequently escaping the attention of our community. The greater the degree of skill, the greater the flexibility and mobility of labour; and mobility of labour is one of the greatest assets in promoting efficiency in industry.
Mr. Chairman, I have concluded my demands upon the time and the patience of this committee. May I add this one, final statement. I believe that every hon. member of this house would agree that the problem of poverty, sickness and injustice in the underdeveloped countries is the problem of Canada. It is in that spirit, and believing that every hon. member of this house shares that view, that I deplore the government's action in the cut-back of their foreign aid program.

Mr. Speaker, as it is the first time that I have the privilege of speaking in this august assembly, I should like to start by joining all those who commended Your Honour while congratulating you on my own behalf for the manner in which you are guiding our discussions in the house.
I also avail myself with great pleasure of this opportunity of telling the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) where my county is located, and what it needs.
When saying that I represent the riding of Quebec West, I am connecting it with the city of Quebec. Of the ten parishes which compose my riding, one section only is part of the upper town, because, on the whole, I represent the lower part of the city, a little more to the north.
Various personalities said: that he who has known and loved Quebec never forgets
Ways and Means
it. Indeed, we should keep in mind that Quebec is the only city in North America, which can boast of still having the ruins of military fortifications and to have been, for more than one and a half century, the whole of Canada, a city where every inch of soil evolves some historic event, and, last but not least, a city which a great traveller placed among the five or six most interesting cities in the whole world.
Also, it was in Quebec that the social and economic movement of this our Canadian nation started. This fine and magnificent riding, with 36,000 voters, is mainly composed of workers, and I am proud to say so here in the house.
Those men and women must work hard for their living. We have among us private industries, and a great many small retailers, for whom I shall stand up this year in the house so that they may obtain fair treatment.
I should like the Minister of Finance to stop a minute and consider, more particularly, what part the small corner grocer is playing. Is it not through the small corner shop that the products reach the consumer's table? Are you aware of the immense effort the corner shops have to make to achieve this? Most of them open their doors at seven o'clock in the morning and remain open till 11 p.m. to meet public demand. Do you know that they are now the only ones to extend credit so that people may eat? And what kind of protection do they get from us? None. If they want somehow to modernize their business there are sudden complications. And so what happens? They mostly buy what they need on instalment plans and have to pay the interest rate you know. As we know that those grocers are only working for a net benefit of 4 per cent a year, why would they not be able to obtain a small loan of some $1,000 to $10,000, for they can supply a reasonable guarantee, though not a guarantee representing ten times the value of their loan? In my opinion, the amounts owed to them and the bills they have on hand to prove it should be accepted as a guarantee for a certain percentage.
Big interests take it upon themselves to call you to order, by bringing pressure to bear. When they want to obtain something, it is very easy: they have the required money. But the small industrialists, the small businessmen do not always have the required capital and the means to pay a competent man

Ways and Means
to defend their right. Yet, those small industrialists have given thousands of jobs to our workers in the past, and in spite of the fight they must carry on against this socialistic current which runs throughout our country, they still want to continue to live according to the same principles, but with more up to date methods. For they have to produce faster to compete with the big industries or chain stores seeking their destruction, and we know very well that in most instances, these big industries belong to foreign capital.
When will the government understand, at last, that there lies part of the wealth of our country, and the only way to cope with the plague of unemployment in Canada?
It is a shame to see so many men and women without work when we know that our country could give employment to and take care of a population five times greater than the one we have now. You can argue that the rate of unemployment is 4.1 per cent or 7 per cent; I maintain that there is absolutely no reason for unemployment in the light of all the work that should be done. Instead of dealing directly with the people to see their hardship, our opponents go by deceitful statistics which no one dares to contest. They prefer to forget, to defend themselves with biting speeches, in an effort to lull the people to sleep. Be careful, opponents, because one day you will face a rude awakening, but it will be too late and you will then have to confess your sins.
We, Social Crediters, want to put order where there is disorder, that is to say put money at the disposal of the people, and not the people at the disposal of money, as it is the case today. The people are patient but when they will have enough, do not forget that you were elected by them, and that they will be the ones to withdraw their confidence in you.
You want to know why we have had so many Social Credit votes? Well, members of the old parties, you just go and spend four or five days behind a counter of a grocery store and you will change your mind, and that will make you more cautious in your remarks on the Social Credit wave which is increasing from day to day. If you have never seen distress at close range, you would see it, and you would realize that families have to work miracles to make both ends meet.
There is another area in which our citizens are not protected, and I mean those famous phony $5, $10 or $20 bills which are circulating more and more these days. It is a constant source of concern for the retailer, and I say it is really unfair that the last

person found in possession of a phony bill should be penalized in losing its value. In my opinion, a special fund should be set up to reimburse merchants who have accepted some of those phony bills, either through carelessness or during rush hours. It is practically impossible for a merchant to keep a constant check on money coming in, especially on week ends.
Mr. Chairman, since June 18 last, you have heard all kinds of things against Social Crediters. Why? If we are really living in a democratic country, as we often like to repeat it, are the people not free to select the men they want, without being insulted by all manners you may think of, and especially the way they have been treated since June 18 last.
You believe, gentlemen of the old parties, that when you come back before the electors and that day is near-to ask for their confidence, they will not remember that? No, gentlemen, you are mistaken. People are not as stupid as you think. With the budgets we are used to having, we end up by feeling sick.
There is one item which is never discussed about the budget, and yet it is the most important. It is the one concerning our debt interest, which is increasing yearly. There is never any discussion about that. Neither is there any effort made to decrease it, everyone is agreed on that point, and yet that is your mistake. We, from this part of the house, should like to draw your attention this year on that situation, and moreover we are suggesting to you the way to correct it; that is what my colleague from Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) has explained to you. If that situation is corrected, how nice it will be to live in this wonderful and vast country of ours. From then on we will be able to say that Canadians are starting to enjoy a normal standard of living, and we shall forever eliminate want in the midst of plenty.
Mr. Chairman, another thing has surprised me since I came to this house, and it was the attitude of our friends on my right. Do you realize that they would have had the utmost difficulty in preparing their speeches if our group had not been represented here this year? And by the way, I would like to tell them that we, from this corner of the house, may not be politicians, but we are happy that we are not. We have freely been elected by the people and for the people.
We are here to act as statesmen, not as politicians. I believe there is a large difference between a politician who has only one thing in mind: how to get re-elected and who

visits his constituents only at the time of the election, and a statesman who works and legislates on behalf of his people every single day of the session.
Mr. Chairman, as long as we have not succeeded in making our fellow Canadians their own masters, you will see us, from this part of the house, standing up for them.
It is unthinkable that foreign capital should take over our country. However, as long as the government will not lower those taxes which dishearten Canadians, the small industrialists and the small home owners, there is no use thinking about alleviating such a situation.
Let us give again confidence to our people through a well balanced economy in using the Bank of Canada, which is empowered with all the necessary authority if the government would only take the necessary measures.
Up to now, we simply managed to see our way through in order to be among the 15 per cent of the people who are entitled to live under this system, and often fraudulently. Is the reason behind this refusal to acknowledge our success, our own refusal to let us be fooled by the trusts and the capitalists we are fighting and our decision to live among the 85 per cent of our people who are neglected by your banking system and who are going into debt in order to live?
If that is what rankles in your mind, wait and see what the future has in store for you. It was said that we were inexperienced, but, gentlemen, did you ever ask yourselves where you acquired your own experience? No, hon. members, we did not come here to put on a show. We came here to defend ideas and principles.
We are for national understanding, but not only in one direction. Justice for everybody and frankness from both racial groups.
Mr. Chairman, according to certain newspapers, one would think that we have become Conservatives. Do you not think that it is a shame? We came here to fight for our rights and we shall defend them before we go back to the people. But we must abide our time and see what this government is willing to do for the people.
I am still a Social Crediter, Mr. Chairman, and I shall continue to be one as long as the present government does not decide to introduce the monetary reform that the popu-
Ways and Means
lation wishes, so that money can be put into circulation in the hands of the consumers in order that the slums so numerous in my district can at last be demolished.
What a shame to think that many families are still without the bare necessaries, that whole families do not eat three square meals a day and do not have decent clothing.
May I suggest to the government a kind of loan for those home owners, similar to the system adopted for the new housing centres. Then, we would see the much needed restoration of hundreds of houses which would make many Canadians happy and would be a credit to our country. Thus, many new jobs could be created, giving our Canadians the opportunity to work, which is their most important right.
If machines are to replace men nowadays, why not reduce working hours to 30 a week, if necessary, since a machine can produce more in less time. Let us pay the same salary to these workers-the goods are there and they will have to be bought. Then we will be able to say that we respect the human being, and our people will have time to develop their knowledge and relax and life will not be so irksome for them.
Under our system, today, individuality is being killed, a great number of heads of families are forced to have a second job to make ends meet.
You may find it funny when we talk about that but when you hear for example the member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather) say that he also believes that what is physically feasible should also be financially feasible, it is different. And yet that is what we have been advocating for more than 30 years.
There is another matter I should like to point out to the Minister of Finance. It is said that to govern is to foresee. Then, what does he intend to do about the young people under 15 who represent almost one third of the population? Would it not be time to train instructors in all sports in general for the benefit of those young people, and set up well organized recreational centres in order to spare them the confusion in which they will find themselves in a few years from now? How many new jobs would thus be provided? It is high time that positive action was taken for the people instead of giving them the impression that they are not wanted in our beautiful Canada which is said to be prosperous.
All this could be done, but, at that, there must be the will to accomplish something. Money is always found somehow to destroy in

Ways and Means
wartime, but for a worthwhile cause in peacetime it is impossible to find. Let us keep in mind that the word "impossible" is the mark of the coward.

Mr. Chairman, it is regrettable that this debate, which has been in progress off and on for the past several days, was somewhat overshadowed for a time by the critical international situation. It is gratifying to us all that the situation has now eased off, and the hope of everybody is that the receding danger of serious consequences will disappear. The crisis, however, should not be considered as an excuse to cover up the urgent need for action to rescue our economy from the doldrums in which it is because of the evident lack of appropriate measures which should have been introduced as soon as danger signals that all was not well with the state of the nation were in evidence.
The Minister of Finance, in his statement on October 22, said in effect that this debate was an extension of the debate started last April, and that it was an important piece of unfinished business. He also pointed out the urgency of the legislation. Well, we of the official opposition did all we could to accommodate the minister in this respect by refraining from prolonging the discussion. However, we failed to convince the other opposition parties that they should comply with that suggestion, but I want to point out, Mr. Chairman, that no one can accuse us on this side of the house of delaying the passing of any legislation.
During his early remarks the minister accused the opposition of downgrading Canada and the Prime Minister. Among other things, the minister said that Canadians are living in the most prosperous year in Canada's history and that our economy is expanding in all directions. There are many people who do not agree with that rosy conclusion. As to the charge that the opposition have been downgrading Canada and have made a deliberate, planned attack on Canada and the Prime Minister, that must be branded as pure nonsense. To my knowledge, no statement was ever made by any member of the official opposition with the intention of downgrading Canada or its Prime Minister. Such statements which have been made by members of the government and its supporters should be treated with the contempt they deserve.
In an editorial about Canadian finances, the Financial Times of October 22 described the situation in this way:
What is revealed is interesting; what is concealed is vital.
That is an abbreviated description of the revised estimates introduced by the Minister

of Finance on October 18. They reveal a reduction of $228 million from the main estimates for 1962-63 which were presented to the house last February by the present Minister Justice, who was minister of finance in the last parliament. The Financial Times correspondent provides in the same issue the widely held opinion that the federal government's deficit for the current year is likely to be at least $600 million, which is much nearer to the $745 million which the former minister of finance announced in the April budget, and the $395 million which was announced by the Prime Minister last June. The obvious reason for this calculation is that revenues are not holding up to the expectation held by the Prime Minister last June.
On this question the editorial had this to say:
This is a far cry from the hopes expressed in Mr. Diefenbaker's announcement of June 24 that the deficit could be cut in the present year to less than $400 million. It demands a drastic revision of the popular expectations aroused by the headlines on Mr. Nowlan's revision of the main estimates.
The objective of a balanced budget, announced by Mr. Diefenbaker in his penitential statements of June 24, and repeated in the speech from the throne on September 27, was never seriously considered as more than a long range project. The cuts in expenditure achieved in the revised estimates show that it is still many years away. Few of them lay the axe anywhere near the root of the tree. Most of them result from pruning the new shoots which will sprout again with renewed vigour each year.
The defence services have been forced to postpone some of their approved plans for new equipment. If the plans were necessary in the first place, they will have to be achieved in double quick time and at double the cost in the coming years. If they were not necessary, as some of them obviously were not, postponement will have the great merit of exposing how silly they were.
Much of the same applies to the freeze on civil service positions. In accordance with a general directive of admirable but wholly misguided intent, government departments are expected to cut their staff budget by 15 per cent through a natural process of attrition. The main result of such a program, unless it is quickly modified, will be to debase the standard of the government service without doing anything to improve its efficiency. On last week's evidence government economy is almost as phony and impermanent as the so-called austerity program.
In view of the opinion voiced by such a responsible publication and many other similar expressions widely accepted by people of diverse political persuasion, and I do not mean amateurs in the field of finance, it is hard to believe that the government intends to go merrily on as though nothing has happened since last April and let the affairs of the nation take their course based on a budget, debate on which was denied to the 24th parliament. Now we are relegated to a debate not on a new budget but on an old budget, and the known economic conditions of the

country when it was brought down bear no resemblance to what has been revealed since.
But, Mr. Chairman, the most objectionable feature of this debate is that it was arranged by the government so as to deny the right of the opposition to move an amendment to the policy of the government. The failure to provide an up to date budget and accounting to the people of Canada as well as an outline of positive action to reverse the present trend of tight money, high interest rates and low national productivity is an added reason why people have lost confidence in the government. I say this notwithstanding the belated announcement by the minister yesterday concerning a new policy regarding automatic transmissions as an aid to the automobile industry. I should like to commend to the government the specific suggestions made by the hon. member for Davenport and others from this side of the house which, if adopted, would give the economy the stimulus needed at this time.
If there is an objective about which the government should be concerned above all others it is to obtain a more productive economy and a higher level of employment, which can be secured by giving attention to the great backlog of needed programs for community development. The Minister of Finance has not made any reference to what I consider a most important proposal, that of creating a municipal development fund or municipal development bank if you wish to call it that, the establishment of which would in no way upset the revised estimates of government spending.
The cost of obligations to municipal governments for the services and facilities which devolve upon them has reached the point where they are taxing their available revenue resources to the maximum. A combination of facts has placed most municipalities in a highly precarious financial position. They have never fully recovered from the deficiency of public services during the war years when they were more or less neglected. The change in population from farms to towns and cities and the increase in over-all population has placed a severe strain on all operations of municipal governments. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the crisis in municipal borrowing presents the municipalities with one of their major problems.
There is a special reason why the federal government should consider the proposal of a municipal development fund. It is the need to co-ordinate capital expenditures, public and private, in the national economy as a whole. Such co-ordination would create the condition of steady growth and stability which is
Ways and Means
vital to the welfare of both public and private enterprise and which, in other words, would mean a measure of co-ordination with respect to actual requirements. The establishment of a municipal development bank would not mean a new policy of subsidy. From a national viewpoint, such a bank would encourage reliance upon domestic savings and facilitate borrowing within Canada for Canadian needs.
We are all painfully aware of what has happened to the municipalities which a few years ago went to the United States to borrow for their needs and now that their loans are maturing are faced with the prospect of paying back in devalued dollars, thus costing the taxpayers of Canada millions of dollars more. The Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities had this to say in one of their submissions to the federal government in 1961:
The establishment of a national municipal lending agency, by removing one of the most frustrating obstacles to municipal development, would give a sharp incentive to the forward planning of growth and redevelopment. It would help greatly to keep constantly before each urban area a planned capital development program which would not only provide work but would direct such work to the satisfaction of basic community needs.
Shelves of public works as an anti-depression program have long been advocated. As the last war drew to a close and unemployment was feared, the advance planning of public works for this purpose was strongly advocated by the federal government in its statement to the dominion-provincial conference of August, 1945. It is particularly significant, moreover, that it advocated that such planning should be undertaken community by community.
This reliance in a democratic manner upon municipal initiative is important. For it is only at the level of the local community that a balanced program representing the needs and desires of local citizens can be developed. Even a large proportion of federal and provincial works, such as roads, bridges, harbour installations, airports and office buildings, must fit into a workable community program in the interest of all concerned.
I wish to point out, Mr. Chairman, that there is nothing novel about this proposal which I am sure a Liberal government would carry into effect. Municipal loan agencies have existed in Europe since the turn of the century and even before. The credit communal of Belgium was formed in 1860 and has been operating successfully ever since. Similar banks or institutions are in existence in Denmark, Holland, Italy, Spain, Switzerland and Turkey, and in the United Kingdom the public works loan board is in many respects a municipal loans bank.
The need for such a federal-municipal loan corporation in Canada is of the utmost urgency and it is in the national interest to have it established at the earliest possible

Ways and Means
moment. It will enable municipal governments to initiate and carry through needed programs of local improvements and redevelopment for which the urgency is very considerable in many municipalities.
The terms of such loans would be as favourable as possible, consistent with the federal government's own cost of borrowing. This would not eliminate the private investor who would still participate in municipal financing by purchasing bonds from the bank or corporation.
The Minister of Finance had a fine opportunity to introduce a measure under the National Housing Act to provide money to purchasers of old houses. Chief Justice Dana Porter, chairman of the royal commission on banking and finance, recently made a statement to the effect that potential buyers of older houses could not arrange financing. There is absolutely no reason why mortgage loans should be denied to people wishing to buy or remodel an old home. I cannot see the sense of restricting insured mortgage loans exclusively to the builders of new homes.
The national house builders association presented a brief to the royal commission on banking, pointing out that people who want to buy an already built house must have a high down payment or take out a conventional mortgage at a high rate of interest, thus discouraging the purchasers of existing houses. The Minister of Finance missed the boat on a scheme which, without costing the government any money, would have stimulated the buying of old houses which invariably would mean extensive improvements on the properties, thus putting a lot of men to work. I suggest also, Mr. Chairman, that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should make direct loans for rental of housing projects in smaller or rural communities, if you will, where it is difficult to get money from banks or mortgage companies. I should like to commend this proposal to the new Minister of Public Works which, if adopted, would expand the area of productive employment.
1 am pleased with the announcement by the Minister of Labour that the municipal winter works incentive program will again be in operation this winter. I may add that while unemployment varies seasonally, being highest in the winter, there is serious unemployment in all seasons. The need is for an all-year employment program of municipal works which would extend both into and beyond the winter season, with provision for scheduling as much of the work as possible to meet the peak periods of unemployment.

One major obstacle to fuller participation in this program by the municipalities is the lack of any provision at the moment for financial assistance toward the cost of materials. Municipalities are willing to embark on capital undertakings which would relieve the unemployment situation considerably if the government were to assume part of the cost of materials in the construction of municipal buildings and other undertakings, and if loans were provided by a municipal development corporation or bank at favourable rates of interest as I indicated a few moments ago. After all, Mr. Chairman, the greatest concern of the moment, as all members agree, is to find ways and means of creating more jobs. I believe it is at this point the government has an opportunity to do something about it.
I am not at all convinced that the curtailment of construction of needed public buildings will materially help the economy. As a matter of fact, it may well have the opposite effect. One consequence of the deletion of government construction is the adverse effect on private enterprise. The psychological implication is obvious. It is a reflection of hard times during which all must economize. The businessman will defer expansion of his business, and he will probably defer construction of a new building. The householder will make the old washing machine do for another year, and so on down the line. The result is that a vicious circle is created and the ranks of the unemployed will grow larger and larger.
It is understood that a budget is designed to provide a policy which will create sufficient revenues to pay fixed and anticipated obligations, and to give every taxpayer a fair deal. We do not question the necessity of imposing taxes which are just and fair and in the national interest. However, there are some which are of a doubtful nature, such as the ten per cent surtax on English china-ware. As everyone knows this is one commodify to which the United States tourist is greatly attracted. However, since the imposition of this tax purchases of English china by United States tourists have been cut by 50 per cent during the last year.
This is a serious matter and is of great concern to the members of the fine china association of Canada. It has had an effect already on employment in stores across Canada, to say nothing of the loss of business, with the net result of a loss of revenue in taxation to the government instead of a gain which this tax was designed to provide. It is a clear case of being penny wise and pound foolish. I suggest, in all sincerity, that a study be made of this matter by the

Department of National Revenue, and the government should give the repeal of this tax serious consideration.
In advanced industrial countries such as Britain, Germany, France and Sweden, national taxation policies are better calculated to be an incentive to industry to invest, sell and expand. According to a news item originating in Birmingham, England, and appearing in yesterday's Globe and Mail, a member of an English trade mission which recently returned from Canada said that Canada is starved for industry. Mr. W. W. Kirk, director of a manufacturing firm said:
Canada needs industry badly and is awakening to the fact that her economy is unsound.
What Canada needs today are men of the calibre of the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe. I firmly believe that when the Canadian people call again upon the Liberal party to form a government, men of that calibre will be in its ranks to direct and lift the economy to its former stable and prosperous climate. The speech by the new Minister of Finance, on the eve of this debate, contained no vision. It was a garbled repetition of statements made by members of the government and its supporters. The only proposal was the creation of an economic development board, with which we do agree and we will support. This revised budget, like its predecessor, is a budget which lacks appeal. It failed to capture the imagination of Canadians to do their best and put their shoulders to the wheel of progress. It is a budget worthy only of a government tottering on the brink, holding to a straw.

Mr. Chairman, the debate so far on this resolution has produced an interesting range of discussion of the current state of the economy and the direction in which it is headed. It is not my purpose in participating in the debate to emulate that whole wide-ranging review. I expect this will be done by the Minister of Finance, when he closes the debate, in order to put much of what has been said in proper perspective. Other ministers have dealt more specifically with subjects under their jurisdiction and my purpose therefore is to deal with some of the matters affecting my own responsibilities as Minister of Public Works, and matters in which I have a direct or indirect responsibility and which have a bearing on the economy.
I do so because I think it is proper that from time to time-what with the mass of ill conceived material, much of it distorted, which is placed on the record by opposition speakers in an attempt to suggest that the economy is stagnating and floundering-to present a true picture so that the country can
Ways and Means
really know what is taking place. Therefore
I	have chosen the field of public works and its related agencies for which I am responsible in order to report something of the progress we have made and something of the prospects for the future, as well as to add this further dimension, this further example of the convincing arguments regarding the general economic health of the country put forward by my colleagues in the debate so far.
Before I come to deal with the activities of my own department I should like to say a few words about the general picture, because from time to time hon. members opposite have made statements, and in some cases produced quotations, designed to suggest that there is no foundation for the position taken by the Minister of Finance and by the government that, while there are still problem areas, nevertheless it is factually correct and indeed encouraging to say that the Canadian economy today is enjoying a period of expansion and buoyancy seldom if ever equalled in its history.
As a basis for my contention I refer to a monthly bulletin entitled Industry put out by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, an organization which has not, over the last year or two, shown any inclination to be unduly favourable to the government. It is true that in this front page article in the bulletin entitled "Forging Ahead" there are some words of caution, but the words of optimism far outnumber them, and there is a general tone of optimism which runs through the whole of the article. I should like to put it on record as an impartial indication and impartial evidence of the validity of the claims we have made. It reads:
How fares the Canadian economy as summer gives way to fall in this year 1962?
The answer is that it is faring very well indeed. Most of the mid-year statistics relating to business and industrial activity are now available and they make impressive reading.
Industrial production in the first six months of this year was up more than 9 per cent on the same period of 1961, likewise manufacturers' shipments. Retail sales were higher by more than 5 per cent.
Output of passenger cars and passenger trucks climbed by more than 30 per cent in the first half of the year, sales by more than 20 per cent. The number of new residential dwellings under construction at the end of July was 9 per cent greater than a year earlier, while the number of completions in the first six months of this year was
II	per cent greater than in the first half of 1961.
When I come to the housing activities for which I am responsible to parliament I shall have more up to date and even more impres-

Ways and Means
sive figures than that to report to the committee.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association publication continues:
The buoyancy of the economy in general-
I ask my hon. friends in opposition to mark those words-
The buoyancy of the economy in general and of manufacturing industry in particular was the reason why there were a record number of Canadians at work at the end of July-180,000 more than a year earlier-and why nearly 50,000 fewer were without employment. Significantly, of those who were looking for a job-4.5 per cent of the total labour force-
Let me interject here that the figure is now down to 3.9 per cent and it is strange, as I have learned, that the more encouraging and the more satisfying is the record of unemployment the louder have been the cries of the opposition that unemployment is at an all time high. The violence and virulence of their attacks increase in inverse ratio to the improvement in the situation. Now, coming back to the quotation:
Significantly, of those who were looking for a job -4.5 per cent of the total labour force-only one in three had been unemployed for more than three months. However, this being the midsummer employment peak, it must be said that the jobless total is still altogether too high for anyone's peace of mind and warrants continuing national concern.
So it does, and that concern is being shown in the progressive measures and the acceleration of the measures designed to increase the expansion of the economy, undertaken by the government. For the information of hon. members I should say those last words are mine and are not a quotation from the publication. Hansard will show where I stopped quoting and where my remarks began.
The article then continues:
Even so, what all this increased business activity means-and we ought surely to recognize it-is that more Canadians than ever before are living better than ever before.
Only the Liberals are worse.

I shall just complete that paragraph so that I will not be accused of distorting anything. I said it included words of caution. It continues:
This is not to say that prosperity is uniform across the land. It isn't and it is not ever likely to be.
The salient feature of the findings of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association is that all this increased business activity means that more Canadians than ever before are living better than ever before.
Mr. Chairman, I have said previously and I repeat that the government cannot and should not claim credit for every single good thing that happens and for every single advantageous development which occurs. We
say our duty is to provide the conditions, the atmosphere, the climate under which, in partnership in enterprise with the Canadian people, our economy can continue the acceleration and expansion which has been going on at an increasing pace over the past year. We do not claim exclusive credit for everything good that happens, but since there seems to be an inclination to lay blame at the door of the government for every adverse situation and difficulty, then occasionally we are entitled to show the country, and particularly hon. members opposite, what the true picture is. To the members of the opposition we are entitled to say "Don't sell Canada short; don't sell confidence. By all means attack government policies where you think they should be attacked but don't attack Canada itself-"
Hear, hear.
-"by constantly representing that things in Canada are worse, or not as they are."
Things could not be worse.

There is a typical example at the moment, Mr. Chairman, an interjection from the Liberal side of the house that things could not be worse. Words almost fail me. The evidence is there before the eyes of the hon. member who made that interjection, but so blinded is he by the political infection from which he and his whole party suffer that their vision is distorted and they are unable to see the true picture. If it were not so almost tragic it would be amusing, but it is a pity to see a once great party, which laid its claim to greatness on its concept of trying to serve Canada, abandon that concept and decide the only thing that matters is trying to get back into power, even if that means adopting the tactic of attacking confidence in the Canadian economy as a whole.
You are crying.

An hon. member opposite says we are crying; but the fact is that the truth is so strange to them that they do not recognize it when it is presented to them, and they interpret it as crying.
However, Mr. Chairman, I said that I did want to deal briefly with some of the activities within the scope of my own department. I would like to come first to the record with respect to building permits. I want to lay before the committee the results of some of the activities the government has been and is carrying out so far as, particularly, they are within the scope of my own responsibility. First, let us look at the area of building permits. The dominion bureau of statistics report dated October 24 states that Canadian municipalities issued building permits-
What year?

Mr. Chairman, I leave it to my hon. friends to live in the past. This government intends to build for the future. The D.B.S. report dated October 24 states that Canadian municipalities issued building permits in August to cover construction estimated at over $238 million, an increase of 8.5 per cent over the year previously. Non-residential construction was larger by 20.1 per cent than the year previously. This is an indication of the measure of business expansion and is an interesting barometer of the rate of progress and expansion in Canada generally. The residential construction permits were down by 2.5 per cent compared with a year earlier, which is not surprising in view of the record pace of the house building boom over the past five years.
I look for particular examples in my own constituency of Kamloops, where there is- and I can assure my hon. friends of this- unbounded optimism and activity in planning for the future. In the city of Kamloops itself the current year will see starts, or plans have been made for starts on various construction projects totalling close to $20 million, among them being a new $4 million civic centre, plans now confirmed for a pulp mill costing $12 million, and a $1 million addition to the oil refinery adjacent to that city.
I cite the activity in Kamloops, of course, because of my close association with it, and also because it is an excellent example of public and private enterprise sharing in progress. In addition to these civic or industrial plans which I have outlined, we have a planned and progressive program of public works construction to meet the needs of a growing community for governmental services. Examples, Mr. Chairman, are the $400,000 R.C.M.P. headquarters building completed last year; a $500,000 high school dormitory for the Indian residential school, now in the process of construction; a $1 million reconstruction and improvement program at the Kamloops airport, and a contract just let for the construction of a federal building costing over $750,000. So here, Mr. Chairman, you have an impressive example of the partnership of government and private enterprise at work and how it works even in some of our smaller communities. It is an impressive and growing record of planning, construction and expansion by industry, matched by a planned and progressive program of construction of new facilities to provide government services for that growing area.
I have, of course, had an opportunity to examine public works projects elsewhere across Canada. I have been to the cities of Toronto; Saint John, Moncton, and Sussex
Ways and Means
in New Brunswick; Hamilton, and Vancouver. I have plans for further inspection of our facilities in Halifax and various parts of Quebec province. I have met some of our officers in the western provinces, as well as in the maritimes, and I hope to be able to undertake a tour of the north country later on. I am impressed with what is going on in Canada, both in regard to public works projects and in housing development, and I am happy with the spirit and the energy of those of our officers and employees whom I have met, who are doing a good job for Canada. Let me tell my hon. friends opposite that these men are doing a good job for Canada. This great number of public servants do not share in their minds and attitudes any of this attitude of doom and gloom and Cassandra prophecy which seems to be exclusive to hon. members of the opposition. With respect to the program-
Mr. Chairman, would the minister permit a question?
-in the current fiscal year-

As you know, Mr. Chairman, time is considerably limited on these occasions. I have a large and impressive program in my department and I should prefer to continue. If I have finished before my 20 minutes is up, I shall be glad to deal with questions.
In the current fiscal year, we are pressing forward-
Mr. Chairman, will the minister not permit a question?

speechtext: Order. Would the hon. member resume his seat, because he is only allowed to ask a question if the hon. member speaking agrees. The minister has indicated that he does not wish to receive a question.

In the current fiscal year, Mr. Chairman, we are pressing forward with such long term programs as the St. John's, Newfoundland, harbour development; a major redevelopment to create a modern harbour for the people of that province and the industries that are based there. This is a $15 million program which has been under way for several years now. It is now near completion. These are examples of partnership with private enterprise for important economic development. Another such project is that at Baie Comeau, where we see a growth of community and where there is a joint development of wharf, storage and harbour improvements with Quebec North Shore Paper, the provincial government and Quebec hydro.

Why are you punishing
Toronto?
Nobody is punishing Toronto.

Mr. Chairman, we have, for instance, such programs as the winter works post offices, under which since 1958 some 258 small post offices in the smaller communities of Canada have been built. These 258 small post offices serve the people of these areas, and they have been built at a cost of some $5 million. Some 50 to 60 more are being planned for construction this winter, thus providing off season jobs for Canadian labour and improvements in the facilities for Canadian citizens.
I should again emphasize, Mr. Chairman, that of course the planning votes have not been touched; the all important vote for preparation, plans and specifications to bring projects from the drawing board stage to readiness for construction are proceeding. Also, this vote is frequently used to acquire sites so that the public works program overall in our planning for the future of Canada is not impaired.
Then in the field of housing, Mr. Chairman, we can say that nowhere is the federal government's investment in Canada's future more apparent and more rewarding than it is here. From 1957 to the middle of 1962 well over
700,000	new homes were built, with the federal government alone investing some $1.5 billion in N.H.A. loans on new residential construction. In the same period direct federal government financing through C.M.H.C. provided 265 long term, low interest loans of almost $160 million for the construction of over 20,000 units of rental accommodation for lower income families and for elderly persons.
Large scale federal-provincial partnership public housing projects have been provided under section 36 of the National Housing Act in growing numbers. Here 75 per cent of the capital costs are borne by the federal government. I mention this particularly, Mr. Chairman, because of something that is frequently

alluded to by members of the Liberal opposition, that they have a blueprint for a program of aid to municipalities. If I had the time to draw together under the compass of one speech all the ways direct and indirect, which through C.M.H.C. and public works we have contributed to the development of all municipal services and municipal housing it would prove a startling and impressive record.

What about shelters in
Toronto?

Mr. Chairman, I should think it is Toronto that needs shelter from the hon. member, more than the other way around. Since 1957, some 6,000 units have been completed.
I can well appreciate how it is that when we take the occasion to state a little of the truth about a glowing record, hon. members on the benches opposite do not really like it. They want to shout it down, but they will never be able to shout down the facts.
Where housing construction is hampered by older and congested buildings and the lack of serviced lots, land assembly projects are undertaken on a federal-provincial basis with 75 per cent of the cost being financed by the federal government. Since 1957, almost 5,000 land assembly projects have been developed.
I should like to have referred to the municipal sewage treatment loans program under which, since 1960, 355 loans have been made totalling $79.5 million and in connection with which we have received 218 preliminary applications having a loan potential of $55.8 million. This program has been of tremendous assistance to municipalities in the provision of new services, and this is the first time such assistance has ever been given.
I have already told the committee that consideration is being given to a number of plans and policies, among them, housing for the handicapped, the provision of loans for the construction of residences for married students and the expansion of our program of municipal loans for sewerage development. At the same time, the department has under review a number of policies designed to increase the value that the public gets from the expenditure of the public works dollar, among them, increased control of expenditures and, perhaps, a more satisfactory basis for the disposition of the numerous claims which are bound to arise as a result of the widespread activity of the department.
These are only a few of the ways in which it could be demonstrated that, contrary to statements by some members of the opposition that this is a government of inaction, the very opposite is the case. More is going on, and will go on in the future, in co-operation

with the other levels of government and with private enterprise to further the expansion of our economy which is, in spite of what is said to the contrary, going on at record rates today.
I should like the minister to tell me, if he can, how many of the winter works post offices were built in the provinces of Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland.
I would have to put that on the record later. Perhaps the hon. member would like to put his question on the order paper.
It is on record in Hansard now.

It is a matter of when I shall have an opportunity to reply. I doubt if I shall have such an opportunity later today. But I should be glad to get those particulars, as I would for any other provinces.
It is easy to answer. It is a small figure.

In view of the fact that the Minister of Public Works during his visit to Toronto was impressed by the work of his department in that city, I should like to ask him why he has refused Toronto federal aid toward building shelters in the underground portion of city hall and, second, why he has cut off N.H.A. mortgages on apartment buildings and reserved them just for his own ministry.
What was that last bit?
Why has the hon. gentleman cut off N.H.A. mortgages in respect of apartment buildings and reserved them for his own discretion?

I do not think the hon. member has the picture at all. I have not refused any assistance to Toronto with respect to the city hall. As to the other suggestion, I can assure the hon. member that as far as I am aware that is far from being the case. Applications are received, and will be processed as they are received. Lending under the National Housing Act is continuing at an impressive level and, as I say, I have plans which, if approved by my colleagues, would lead to a further expansion in certain areas.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to try to match the wide range of the speech the minister has just given. I want to deal with one aspect of the matter which is not so rosy as the general picture which the minister has painted. I enter this debate briefly for one purpose only. I desire to point out, with reference to one particular industry, the tremendous importance of economic planning by the government and others directly concerned.
Ways and Means
I refer to the aircraft industry and, in particular, to the plight of the employees of Canadair Limited which was referred to yesterday on the orders of the day. Most hon. members will be aware that Canadair Limited is the largest aircraft producing company in Canada and it has been described as one of the most progressive of the small group of aircraft producers which make up the aircraft industry in this country. Since January 1 of this year there has been a steady and drastic reduction of the work force. In all, 2,400 employees have been laid off. A further 1,100 employees are slated to be laid off before the end of the year. This makes a total of a 54 per cent cut in the work force of this company. Lay-offs have now reached down to men with 12 years seniority and will soon reach those with 15 years seniority.
This loss of employment means a drastic reduction in the payroll and a consequent loss to merchants. The international association of machinists, in a brief which some hon. members may have read, says this will mean making Montreal into a depressed area. This may be exaggerating the situation. It will certainly make for a lot of depressed homes in that city. Moreover, these lay-offs mean the loss of skilled workers to the aircraft industry and an increased dependence on the United States and other foreign countries where aircraft are manufactured. The indirect result of this substantial reduction in our aircraft industry will affect many suppliers in other businesses. I leave it to members of this committee to consider what it means to the individual lives of the employees who have been laid off, and to the lives of their families.
How can government help? In April of this year, the Canadian Labour Congress in its annual presentation to the government made a recommendation, among others, calling for the establishment of an air transport industry council composed of representatives of government, aircraft producers, air lines and interested trade unions to review and anticipate aircraft needs in Canada. I may say in passing that the trade union concerned with Canadair, the international association of machinists, is a highly respected and responsible union which on May 5 of next year will be celebrating its 75th anniversary. As far as I understand it, the recommendation for the setting up of this air transport industry council has not been accepted or acted upon by the government. It seems to me that had it been acted upon, the council might have been in a position to make recommendations to the government leading to steps which would have prevented the substantial lay-offs which I have described.
I am not qualified to discuss the technical aspects of what should be done, or to suggest

Ways and Means
what guarantees or subsidies may be required in order to preserve this vital industry. However, it does seem to me that India's need tor help in the present border conflict requires a review of the situation in the Canadian aircraft industry. In these circumstances the answer given yesterday in this house to the hon. member for Laurier by the Minister of Defence Production does not seem sufficient. It is true that India may not require the CL-44's which are manufactured by this particular company; but if, for example, India wants a particular type of plane, such as the Caribou plane, and the productive capacity is limited, would it not be possible to direct the attention of the Indian government to the possible suitability of the CL-44's as a proven transport plane?
Indeed, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the R.C.A.F. itself might review its requirements for transport planes at the present time. We all know that this government is committed to what we call a program of austerity, but I question whether austerity should extend to essential defence needs, especially if the result would undermine the efficient operation of a key industry such as the aircraft industry. If, Mr. Chairman, after a careful review of what can be done for the aircraft industry, and this company in particular, no steps can be taken by the government to stop lay-offs at this particular plant, have the government made any particular plans to absorb elsewhere the unused skills of the workers who will be laid off?
I suggest that this problem cannot be left to the haphazard workings of the labour market, but requires careful economic planning. Of course, the loss of a key Canadian industry, or a reduction in its capacity, needs to be considered, as well as the economic circumstances of the particular industry. Mr. Chairman, the problems of the aircraft industry and its employees are only an illustration of the wider needs for economic planning generally. It is quite impossible to cope adequately with the problems of full employment, economic growth and expansion without close co-operation between the government, labour and industry, and with purposeful planning. The apparent complacency of the Minister of Finance-and I stress the word "apparent" because I am sure there is no real complacency-about the economic situation in Canada is not shared by the skilled workers of Canadair Limited, and I suggest a new approach is needed. Mr. Chairman, the Canadian nation like all other nations in the world, went through the whole gamut of emotions during these last few years. We saw the president of the United States courageously oppose

the construction, right at the door of his own country and of ours, of Soviet launching bases, the use of which was surely not for protecting the Cuban territory, and still less for ensuring peace. The world was shocked to learn that despite previous denials by Russians and Cubans, Russia had effectively started to instal such launching bases on the Cuban territory.
The free world supported the American government in its decision to impose quarantine around the island of Cuba in order to prevent Soviet missiles from entering it. Nevertheless, this action did not keep all nations from fearing the worst. The action taken by President Kennedy was necessary, but we all knew that if both parties could not come to an understanding, a world war could ensue, a war capable of destroying the human race.
Quite fortunately, the action taken by President Kennedy set the facts straight for the world and especially the Soviet block. The president's courage bore fruit because the Soviet prime minister saw the light, admitted his wrongs and ordered the dismantling of the missile bases under construction in Cuba, with U.N. supervision.
President Kennedy, following an exchange of notes with Mr. Khrushchev, said that both of them, due to their heavy responsibilities as regards the maintaining of peace, were aware that the situation had reached a point where events could have gone out of control. President Kennedy further stated that he was prepared to examine as soon as possible the problem of disarmament in a constructive spirit, in Geneva or anywhere else.
Without entertaining any illusion, we can still have the highest hopes, after the events that just unfolded.
Men of good will all over the world are asking that the armament race be stopped and, for logical as well as humanitarian reasons, that all countries agree to proceed with a disarmament based on understanding, because the world is threatened with destruction, and that it be done under the supervision of the United Nations, which once again have shown their usefulness as an instrument of peace.
The international events which we have just witnessed, serious though they may be, should not make us forget that we have to keep on looking after the nation's business, which is our business. That is why, for a few minutes, I should like to deal with the problems we have to face immediately.

But, prior to that, in keeping with tradition, I wish to congratulate the Speaker of this house as well as the Deputy Speaker and chairman of committees. My congratulations also to the new ministers, to the cabinet members who have been promoted, and my condolences to those who have lost something there.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF GROUNDS SET OUT IN 1930 STATUTE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the Divorce Act, 1930, be amended by extending the grounds for which a divorce a vinculo matrimonii may be granted so as to include desertion for three years, legal cruelty, and incurable insanity.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to move this resolution for the consideration of the house. It is a resolution which, if it should happen to pass, would really go a long way toward the process of bringing our laws on divorce from the 19th into the 20th century. From the point of view of hon. members of the house who are engaged in the practice of law and are associated with the whole field of divorce law, one thing has impressed us, or certainly has impressed me, has been the tremendous social hardships, the great personal anguish, and the tales of human tragedy and unhappiness that result from the unfairness and the backwardness of our divorce laws in this country. In surveying divorce laws throughout the western world it is actually trite to say that Canada's divorce laws are among the most restrictive in the whole of the western world. As all hon. members know, in those provinces where divorce is available the only ground is adultery, except for the province of Nova Scotia where cruelty is also a ground. As has been pointed out, the purpose of the resolution is to extend the grounds for divorce so as to include three years desertion, legal cruelty and incurable insanity.

Private Bills
If I may say a word about the problem of adultery as the sole ground. From the debates which have taken place previously in the house it is obvious that it is a difficult charge to prove, although I do not feel that collusion is as prevalent as some hon. members have led the house to believe. But the important thing about adultery is that it is rarely the real cause of the breakdown of the marriage. Quite the contrary takes place in actual fact for it is usually something that follows a marriage that is already shattered and has already broken apart.
There are many marriages where a single act of adultery has not resulted in the breakup of the marriage because the parties to the marriage have been able to reconcile their differences, patch up their marriage and continue on their way. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the family courts of Canada from coast to coast are filled with a stream of unhappy people whose marriages are hopelessly shattered but who, because they do not have the technical, legal ground of adultery, remain married to each other.
As I have said, this resolution will bring our divorce laws into the 20th century. It is important to note that most of our provinces have pre-confederation divorce laws, Nova Scotia in 1866, New Brunswick in 1791 with some amendments, Prince Edward Island in 1835, Quebec and Newfoundland with no divorce courts at all, British Columbia and the prairies in 1858 and Ontario having the law of England as of July 15, 1870. What I am trying to point out is that the world has changed since those times, that our knowledge is more up to date, that our community life has changed, that our knowledge is more in the modern sphere and what is needed is a new look at the whole problem of the divorce laws.
Prior to moving this resolution, Mr. Speaker, I had occasion to examine the debates of the house. It is interesting and encouraging to read in the debates views expressed by many hon. members with regard to divorce and its grounds that go far beyond the views expressed in this resolution. Also, Mr. Speaker, outside this house there are bodies of opinion throughout Canada, enlightened individuals and groups everywhere who are cognizant of the need to bring our divorce laws up to date.
Indeed, the real problem is not whether to reform our divorce laws but rather how to accomplish this desirable end. The real problem is that our marriage ceremony is both a legal and a religious ceremony and gives rise to both legal and religious rights and duties. The real opposition comes from those individuals who regard the religious

aspect as everything and take the view that civil rights cannot override the insolubility of the religious tie. If we deal with the matter on this very narrow basis their view is unanswerable, but what it does do is that it disregards the whole problem of the civil rights and duties arising from marriage such as support, custody, mutual help and society and children. It denies to the subjugated majority their right to differ. It fails to face the fact that our divorce laws no longer meet the views and the needs of the majority of Canadians. This is really our essential problem.
Our reluctance for political or any other reasons to offend those people who are opposed to any change in the status quo denies to the majority of Canadians the right to bring the laws up to date and to make them accord with modem ideas and methods. It is against this barrier of method, rather than need, that progress has stopped.
It may be that there is no possibility of a uniform law for all of Canada. Certainly the sentiments of those of the Catholic faith throughout Canada who feel that no divorce at all is possible must receive consideration, although I feel that this view may be exaggerated and has on occasions been exploited for political advantage. The views of such a large body of opinion must receive consideration just as, at the same time, the views, needs and desires of the rest of Canada are entitled to consideration and action.
Second, Mr. Speaker, there are great constitutional problems. The constitutional power of divorce rests in this house; but the method of procedure, the question of alimony, the custody of the children and so on is left with the provincial legislature. There are, therefore, constitutional problems that have to be solved as well.
Then, there are regional differences that have to be taken into consideration. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, in attempting to deal with this very real social problem one is impressed with the fact that the subject is so complex, the issues are so mixed, both from a religious and social point of view, the need for understanding and change is so great, the injustice of our present laws is so evident and the misery that our inadequate law provides now is so pronounced, that one realizes it cannot be dealt with in the one hour at our disposal.
While the discussion which does take place here is useful, in that we have the views of the members on this matter, after watching this one hour go by on various occasions I have a suspicion that this resolution probably will not come to a vote. In view of the necessity of dealing with this social problem,

if by chance this resolution does not pass, I would earnestly urge the government to set up a royal commission in Canada to study the whole question of marriage law, family law and divorce. Let its terms of reference be broad. Let it hear views from all parts of Canada and all groups in Canada interested in this problem. Let it study the laws in other countries and the effects good or bad of those laws. Let it study the need for constitutional reform and jurisdictional problems. Then, let it report to this parliament, either in the next session or the session after or to the next parliament, if that be the case. This matter can be dealt with in this way.
I know all the objections to royal commissions. But surely, Mr. Speaker, this subject is so vast, so complex and so difficult that a royal commission would serve a useful purpose. For example, it would meet I am sure the very difficult problem that faces this house in connection with divorces from the other place. I know that if a broad royal commission were set up a lot of the difficulty could be eliminated. This would give all religious groups, all social groups, an opportunity of presenting their point of view. The establishment of a commission has been supported by religious bodies, by women's organizations and by social organizations throughout Canada. What I am trying to say, Mr. Speaker, is that there is a great body of thought in Canada that wants a reappraisal of this whole field. A fresh, comprehensive look at the whole field of marriage law is required. This problem affects the lives of all.
The failure to make a good marriage can be the end of the trail for many young couples. It can mean failure to achieve a place in the world, a failure to make the best use of your talents, a failure to make a proper contribution to society or to find a place in society. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion I should like to say that the tensions we have experienced this week may well make members feel the problems of divorce are really not too important. However, as one person who has worked in this field for some years I can assure you that to those who are concerned with this problem the need is very real. These marriage problems distort and affect the daily lives of the people who experience them. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if this minority government could take action and either pass the resolution or set up a royal commission, it would give leadership, hope and help to that not inconsiderable body of public opinion that looks to us in their hour of need. It is in this spirit and with this hope that I recommend this resolution to the house.
