speechtext:
I am
happy to be able to say a few more words on this subject which came before the house on a previous occasion by way of a bill and which is before us today by way of a resolution. I was quite pleased to hear the hon. member for Danforth refer to the setting up of a royal commission. I am in complete agreement with that. Whenever we have a contentious or difficult problem, then the best way to gather all points of view is to set up a royal commission. Then, you can arrive at a proper decision. This Conservative government believes in this procedure, so I support his reference to that.
In so far as the resolution is concerned, I should like to repeat what I said briefly on a previous occasion. I think if it is right to have a divorce law at all in Canada it should be one that serves the average individual better than the law does now. When we are extending the grounds for divorce, we must not forget the very purpose of marriage. It is to raise a family, to educate that family and create good citizens. In this connection, I should like to quote from an article entitled "The Rights of Children", published in "Vital Speeches of the Day", I quote:
The emotional health of the children of divorced homes is a far more mysterious and complex problem than is the issue of their economic and educational rights. The children of separated homes, where a cold war continues between the ex-spouses, will have serious adjustments to make. Psychologists who are becoming ever more familiar with the problem of the child with two homes tell us that the emotional impact of such a situation upon youngsters is simply enormous.
Perhaps some child as perceptive as Anne Frank will arise to describe the tensions, conflicts and emotional upheavals that come to a child from having a week end father and a week long working mother.
I might pause here to say that is one important reason for advocating the establishment of a royal commission. I refer to the fact that there are many problems connected with this subject and there are many different viewpoints. There are many children who have been raised in torn homes who are emotionally disturbed, and when they reach maturity in later years this emotional disturbance has an impact on their life.
The central issue of the emotional rights of children centres on the question of visitation privileges

Private Bills
for the person not having custody. The law has given very little thought to this matter and has simply assumed that a father has an inherent right to see his child. It is not even certain whether the right to visitation exists in the child or in the father or in both.
At least a few students of the matter have questioned the advisability of any visitation rights to the father in particular cases. It would appear that the emotional equipment of some children is simply incapable of handling an inherently complex situation. This is particularly so in the cross currents of multi-relationships which arise when both the mother and the father remarry and have children by their second spouses.
The law can hardly be expected to know very much about the unknown sea of the emotional life of children with week end fathers. Would the appointment of an impartial arbitrator be worthy of consideration? Such an arbitrator would be removed from the adversary proceedings of the parents, would have special training in the psychology of children with week end fathers. Would the ap-sult which would not be determined by the accidents of litigation but rather based on the inherent rights to emotional security which all children possess.
The conclusion he reaches is this:
The rights of all children to economic, educational and emotional security should, therefore, be the prime objective of law and society whenever the courts must make a decision affecting the life and future of children.
After all when we have these divided homes, divided by order of the court or by agreement of the parties, then the paramount consideration must be the children. Therefore I feel that in considering this whole problem we should give the most serious consideration to the children themselves. I am sure there are many of us who have had the opportunity to walk into city police cells in various places, in this country and other countries, and have found teenagers who have run foul of the law. In many cases it is not the children who should be on trial. Many times it is parents who should be on trial because it is the emotional disturbances the children have suffered, during the time they were raised and educated by their parents, that have brought about the situation which led them to come before the courts of justice.
With respect to the grounds for divorce, I should like to repeat that I do not think we should make divorce too easy. Whatever we do in this regard to make the law of divorce practical, we should make certain there is a time period from the date of marriage until the date that either spouse could petition to go before the courts of justice to have the marriage dissolved, and I believe that time period should be five years rather than three. That would create the necessary precaution in the minds of people before they enter into the relationship of marriage.
We should also support the pre-marital clinics to assist young people in coming to a decision to accept the proper responsibilities

of marriage, and that is why I welcome, as an individual member, the suggestion that we should have that period so that they cannot get married on Tuesday and go into the divorce courts on Thursday.
It is always interesting to hear the socialists because they feel they are great reformers; but one should take a look at the province of Saskatchewan where we have the only socialistic experiment in government on this continent. It is far more difficult to obtain a divorce in the province of Saskatchewan than it is in the province of Alberta, even though the grounds are identical, the jurisdictions as to domicile are identical, the things which must be proven are identical, but not the procedure.
Saskatchewan has a most cumbersome procedure. First of all an action must be started by a statement of claim. Prior to the issue of the statement of claim the plaintiff in question, the spouse seeking the relief, must secure a particular affidavit called an affidavit of bona fide. After that is filed before the court the statement of claim must not only be served on the opposite spouse but also on the respondent, and if it is an undefended action the procedure is the same as if it were a defended action. Notice of trial must be personally served, or served through double registered mail, on the various parties.
That procedure is very cumbersome as compared with the situation in the province of Alberta. The procedure there in reference to divorce is similar to that in any other undefended action. A statement of claim is issued and then, after waiting a period of time for a reply, the plaintiff can go before the courts. In fact it is possible to start an action for divorce on a Friday and be before the courts in Alberta on the following Monday, while in Saskatchewan it may be six months before the proceedings come before a court. In fact I believe the reformers should start in the homeland from which they spring because, as I have outlined, the procedure there is very cumbersome and difficult.
With respect to grounds for divorce, I endorse the resolution so far as extending the grounds are concerned because when it comes to the proof of adultery, it is something, as one distinguished counsel once said, which never occurs with threes. Therefore for the courts to accept proof they must draw certain inferences. Sometimes when the evidence is very strong the court may draw the inference that it is so strong that the parties may not be telling the truth, and sometimes when the evidence is weak the court may draw the inference that it is too weak.
I appreciate the fact that the evidence presents a difficult problem. I may add that

when the liberal judges, speaking with a small "1", in some jurisdictions have drawn inferences, and drawn them broadly, in a sense they have made it easier to prove adultery even on that one ground. It is quite a hardship sometimes for people to come into court themselves, if the evidence is there, and make certain admissions. It is like hanging your dirty linen on the line, and I say that if it is right to have a divorce law in Canada it is right to have one that will properly serve the individual seeking that remedy. That is why I support the grounds of desertion for three years.
Then there is the question of legal cruelty. Legal cruelty would mean cruelty as defined by the courts, and the courts have already given decisions on it. Then also incurable insanity is a reasonable ground for divorce but I still preface my remarks by saying there should be a waiting period, because there is the sanctity of the home and of marriage itself to be considered. Coming back to what I said in the beginning, the most important thing is the home, the raising and education of children so that they will turn out to be good citizens for Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I can clear up the burning question of the moment as to what constitutes cruelty as a ground for divorce, since this is one of the two grounds we recognize in Nova Scotia in divorce proceedings. In that respect we are unique in Canada.
There are two aspects of cruelty which would entitle a court in Nova Scotia to dissolve a marriage. One is prolonged physical violence towards one of the spouses so that that spouse is in danger of departing into the beyond if the physical violence continues. The second aspect deals with mental cruelty, but this is not of the variety we hear about in connection with movie star divorces.
Mental cruelty, as recognized in Nova Scotia, is cruelty suffered by one member of the marriage to the degree that that member is in danger of being driven from sanity to insanity. Thus a tremendous burden is imposed on the person invoking cruelty as a ground for divorce, and the number of such 27507-3-74
Private Bills
applicants is very small in any one year. I would venture to guess there would not be more than five or six.
Before I proceed to discuss the resolution presented to us by the hon. member for Dan-forth I wish to compliment him for his great sincerity in his approach to this difficult problem. We have heard an hon. member from that corner speaking with all his heart for the people whose problems he is concerned with, and also with a mind for the very difficult problems that divorce presents to Canadians. I must say I found his speech refreshing and most interesting, mainly because he did not minimize the difficulties that face Canadians in the divorce field.
The three grounds the hon. member has presented have been considered on occasion by the Canadian Bar Association. Perhaps an indication of the delicacy of this problem and how Canadians are loath to face up to it is the fact that only once, I believe, in the recent history of the Canadian Bar Association has a resolution on divorce passed that body. This is despite the fact that every day lawyers are concerned with the way the practice of divorce is carried on, and every day across Canada good lawyers are refusing to enter courts to handle divorce actions because they feel there is a stigma attached thereto. One would think, therefore, the Canadian bar might have been able to come to better grips with this subject. It did so, I believe in 1954, at the meeting in Winnipeg, at which it suggested the three grounds for divorce contained in the resolution presented by the hon. member. I believe the bar association also added that these grounds apply in particular provinces desiring them; this perhaps to get around the problem that certain provinces would not wish to enlarge the grounds for divorce.
As for the grounds themselves, they are all eminently sensible ones and, I think, most suitable as a partial answer to this problem. With regard to desertion for three years, it has been estimated that some 50,000 Canadian women are the victims of desertion for this period. Therefore you can see, Mr. Speaker, that a sizeable number of helpless creatures would be helped if this were a ground. Desertion, of course, is the poor man's method of obtaining a divorce; simply to hie away from house and hearth.
The second ground is incurable insanity. While the hon. member did not define it, I am sure that as a very careful lawyer he probably has in mind the practice that prevails in the United Kingdom and elsewhere, where very careful hedges are put about this ground of incurable insanity. This is because, after all, we do now recognize that the incurably insane of today may be cured by wonder

Private Bills
drugs tomorrow and be perfectly sane again. It has been found that, if there is to be a cure for insanity, it generally occurs, in at least 90 per cent of the cases, within a three year period, I believe. If a person is incurably insane for more than that time, there is little hope of cure in the future. I think incurable insanity, if it is understood that there be safeguards written into the law, would be a good ground.
Then legal cruelty is the hon. member's third ground. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) could have regaled the house with the leading case on this subject from the province of Nova Scotia; but since he did not, I shall. It concerns an event on a bitter December night in the south end of Halifax. A young lady was incensed with her husband and she rushed forth into the night, packed snowballs and threw them through the living room window at her husband, who was seated in front of a roaring fire. The young lady was so overwrought that she had rushed forth without an overcoat or overshoes; she was standing there in her ordinary clothing, packing these snowballs and throwing them at her husband. He, as I say, was seated in quite comfortable circumstances except for the fact that he had to duck about from time to time to avoid the snowballs.
The husband applied to the courts for a divorce on the ground of cruelty. He said to the judge that it was cruel of his wife to throw snowballs at him. The judge pondered this case for some time and eventually reached a decision that, if there was cruelty, it surely must have been cruelty toward the young woman, who had to stand outside in such chilling weather and such uncomfortable circumstances; it certainly was no cruelty to the husband, who did have a nice warm seat by the fireplace. So the case was thrown out. Hon. members of the house who are lawyers may wish to investigate that case, and they will find it reported in the Dominion Law Reports, somewhere around 1947, I believe.
It was suggested here this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, that a royal commission should study the problem of divorce and the related law and problems dealing with families and children-custody, maintenance, and what have you. I ordinarily would not welcome a royal commission approach to this problem. I think we have hon. members with sufficient experience and knowledge to tackle the problem within our own house, so to speak; and we could be joined by gentlemen from the other place, some of whom have also had a great deal of experience in the field of divorce.

As I say, Mr. Speaker, ordinarily I would not welcome a royal commission approach to this problem, but it commends itself for one very good reason. It seems to me it is the best way to confront all the different camps on this matter of divorce; those in favour of large reform, those in favour of medium reform, and those against any reform or change whatsoever. A royal commission would give a chance for all these differing points of view to be heard. I think that is important, because I find, in discussing this matter with Canadian audiences-and I think I made 40 speeches to Canadian clubs on this subject last year-that it generally took about 50 or 60 minutes to even put the problems in perspective. Once this was done, it was much easier to sell the idea of divorce reform. Perhaps the hon. member for Dan-forth will agree with me on this.
One of the concerns of those who are against divorce reform-and I think we had an opinion from the other side of the house the other day which is a perfect example-is that the present state of the divorce law has made Canadians wary of further changes. The present law, I submit, sir is so bad in some respects that those opposed to reform can say, "Well, look; you have already got a bad situation. If you make any further changes, then we are going to have further bad situations". So it was that I suggested the other day in another divorce debate that we should take a new look at the one ground that is prevalent across Canada today, the ground of adultery, to allow divorce, in my submission, where the adultery is on a continuing basis. In other words, this would be where a marriage has broken up and one of the parties has gone off to live with somebody else. It would knock out the isolated act of adultery as a ground for divorce and would substitute -and this was the submission I made the other day-separation for a period of not less than three years. The virtue of this is that it would provide the cooling-off period that I think is essential when we face this problem. There have been cases where people have hastily rushed to a divorce court after a trivial quarrel. Sometimes they have been held back by sweet reason setting in later on. Apparently, you cannot do that in Alberta, because if you start a divorce action on a Friday you might wind up on Monday divorced. So I must quarrel with the rather astringent observations of the hon. member for Bow River as to the practice in Saskatchewan. I do not know whether the law should be cumbersome, but at least delay does provide for a cooling off period which, apparently, does not prevail in the hon. member's own province of Alberta.

These thoughts having been unburdened, may I say in summation that I compliment the hon. member on a reasoned introduction of his resolution. I think his grounds are fine ones, and his suggestion of a royal commission study, which has been supported by the hon. member for Bow River, commends itself to me as one way in which a good, open discussion of this vital problem could be had.

I realize that the hon. member who introduced this motion has a deep interest in the subject of divorce and in welfare matters generally, because the first time I had the privilege of meeting him was in a family court shortly after the election in June. I also realize that there has been an approach to this question today, as has just been mentioned by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave), which we have not formerly seen coming from the party to which the sponsor belongs. I am afraid that for the last few years we have been accustomed to hearing from that quarter remarks which were not always complimentary toward the legal profession. I appreciate very much that the new party is now graced with at least four members of our profession who may have a tempering influence on the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). At least, the new approach may help balance some very unusual statements we used to hear from time to time. I do not, by this, detract in any way from the efforts of those hon. members, but I do hope we shall have a slightly more reasoned approach to this subject in future.
It is trite to say that the subject of divorce has been discussed in this house ad nauseam for the last five years at least and, undoubtedly, for many years prior to that. However, to a large extent the previous discussions have been concerned with procedure rather than with divorce itself, and the grounds which should be admitted. We are becoming aware that there are a number of separate problems raised by divorce each of which must be dealt with separately. This motion today, dealing particularly with the grounds for divorce in provinces to which the divorce act applies, represents a somewhat new subject and one which deserves our careful consideration.
There are three grounds set out in this resolution, and I think they are very worthy grounds which the divorce act could be extended to cover. However, in the first place, I think desertion after three years might not always be sufficient grounds for divorce. If there is clear and final evidence of desertion for three years the courts should have no difficulty, but I am afraid that if the period 27507-3-74J
Private Bills
were limited to three years in a number of cases, there might be an opening for desertion purely for the purpose of securing a divorce. I should like to see any legislation which might be brought in in this connection make it very clear that the grounds for desertion have to be well established and bona fide and should not amount merely to a person going away for that period of time in order to secure the dissolution of marriage.
The second ground mentioned, legal cruelty, has been discussed this afternoon and I have spoken on this particular matter on several previous occasions. The phrase "legal cruelty" and, more particularly, "mental cruelty" has always bothered me. I am sure that mental cruelty is one of the things which would be covered by this resolution, and I have always been afraid that if it were accepted as grounds for divorce we should be extending those grounds beyond what is reasonable and proper. Again, this would be a matter of definition within the legislation, and if legislation were drafted, and if mental cruelty were included as a ground for divorce, I should want to see it very narrowly defined so that the type of ground for divorce we often find in certain other jurisdictions would not appear in Canadian courts. I believe, however, that the answer which has been given to this argument at different times is that our courts would not lightly go beyond a reasonable definition of mental cruelty.
We are dealing here with divorce in provinces where divorces are granted by the normal courts in those provinces. As always, the problem of the children arises. When there is a divorce in the provincial courts, those courts are at the same time seized with the matter of the custody and maintenance of the children, if any. I think this is particularly necessary if we are going to talk about an expansion of the grounds for divorce.
The interests of the children should come first in any discussion of this problem. However, there is an advantage in enlarging the grounds, particularly with regard to desertion. So often we find that a deserted wife has been left with the children. Sometimes, of course, they are left with the husband; but most often it is the wife who is deserted. Not only is she left without support, but she is left without any knowledge of what is likely to happen in the future. The question of custody of the children remains unsettled, so long as there is no divorce, and the question of the wife's legal status is also left unsettled. Recently I came across something which surprised me in connection with the employment of married women who are separated from their husbands and who have not obtained a divorce. I have discovered several

Private Bills
employers who will not employ a married woman separated from her husband unless she has either a legal or written separation or a divorce. The reason behind this seems to be that the woman will be in a state of mental upset, and there is danger that the husband may come to the place of employment and cause distress both to the wife and to the employer. While I think that is unfair, it is also one ground for settling once and for all the status of a woman who has been definitely and finally deserted. I think, under those circumstances, that the expansion of the grounds to cover desertion is very well warranted.
Mr. Speaker, it has often been said that the ground behind a divorce is a breach of the marriage contract, and certainly adultery is a breach of the marriage contract. But if we look at the others, we also find that desertion and cruelty are breaches of the marriage contract, or the marriage undertakings which were made at the time of the marriage. For example, the vow, in most cases, to be true to each other "till death do us part" is not just to be true in the sense of faithfulness, but also in the sense of supporting one's spouse in sickness and in health, and so forth. Therefore, desertion and cruelty might very well be considered, and in most cases definitely are, breaches of those undertakings which husband and wife made at the time of their marriage.
Incurable insanity, of course, is not a breach of those marriage vows because it is something that has happened, presumably, beyond the power of the husband or wife, unless it be the case that one party or the other was so difficult that either he or she brought on such incurable insanity. But aside from that, incurable insanity is not the fault of either of the parties in most cases. Nevertheless, if it is shown to be absolute and final, then I think such ground would be proper. I think that in the case of a young couple great care should be taken with regard to insanity, because, as has already been stated, the parties, or one of them, may be sent to a place where, because of advances in medical science-and these advances are being made daily-that party will recover his or her sanity. However, I think there are types of incurable insanity which can be verified, and such things as senility which has reached an advanced stage, or similar types of insanity which are incurable, might very well be considered suitable grounds.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I would say this. I believe that the general feeling that divorce should not be made easier is one with which I agree. We in this country do not want to have easy divorce. But this is not inconsistent

with enlarging the grounds of divorce to those which have been set out in this resolution. If they are carefully drafted and carefully supervised, I see no reason why they should result in any great expansion of the divorce rate in Canada; it will simply mean there are more cases which are proper cases and which deserve the attention of the courts. I think, under those circumstances, that the general principle set out in this resolution should be accepted.

Mr. Speaker, I see that
the time consumed by the speakers who have preceded me, and who have been deeply interested in this fundamental problem, does not leave me too much time now. However, I know that there are many others interested in this subject who want to speak, and I hope that this question will come up again for further discussion. One of the hon. members on the other side, I think the hon. member for Cartier, made some inquiry as to what the hon. member for Danforth had in mind when he defined "legal cruelty". Of course, it is very difficult to define. Legal cruelty has been the subject of consideration by many judges and courts both in Canada and England, and I think it is one of those things you had best experience. I would suggest to the hon. member, as we have been exposed to a long dissertation from his side of the house, that if he would come over to this side of the house at some time he might have a better idea of what is legal cruelty.
Mr. Speaker, I have time to make only this one observation. In considering this question, while there is a problem as far as a fairly large number of people are concerned, it is one which must generally yield to the necessity of the many. I would hate to see legislation adopted which would have the effect of making it easier to slip in and out of divorce, as one slips in and out of one's overcoat. This is a deep social problem fundamentally affecting the state. I think it has been established through history that when you see the disintegration of the family you see the deterioration of the state. I feel that this question should be subjected to a great deal of contemplation before we proceed to make things too easy and too simple for people to secure divorce.
